cards.title: What is E2E Testing?
cards.content:
End-to-End (E2E) testing is a methodology used to test whether the flow of an application is performing as designed from start to finish.

Unlike unit testing, which tests functions or individual components in isolation, E2E testing ensures that all integrated parts of your React application—including the frontend, router, global state, API, and database—work together seamlessly.

Why React developers need it:

  • Ensures critical user paths (like signup, checkout, and search) are never broken.
  • Tests real user interactions on simulated modern browsers.
  • Provides high confidence before deploying to production.

content.question: Which of the following is a primary characteristic of End-to-End (E2E) testing compared to Unit testing?

options.text: It tests individual React components and utility functions in isolation without a browser environment.
It verifies the integrated flow of the entire application, running it in a real or simulated browser.
It is significantly faster to execute and has zero network dependency.
It is used exclusively to test the CSS styling of components.

cards.title: Cypress vs Playwright
cards.content:
In the modern React ecosystem, two tools dominate E2E testing: Cypress and Playwright.

Cypress

Cypress runs directly inside the browser. It is incredibly developer-friendly, provides time-travel debugging, and is highly visual.

cy.visit('/login');
cy.get('[data-testid="email"]').type('user@test.com');
cy.get('button').click();

Playwright

Developed by Microsoft, Playwright runs out-of-process. It is known for outstanding multi-tab, multi-origin support, parallel execution speeds, and modern auto-waiting features.

await page.goto('/login');
await page.getByTestId('email').fill('user@test.com');
await page.getByRole('button').click();

cards.title: Robust Selectors in React
cards.content:
When targeting elements in React, avoid CSS classes (e.g., .btn-primary) or dynamic CSS-in-JS selectors (like those generated by Styled Components or CSS Modules) because they change frequently and break tests.

The Golden Rule: Use dedicated testing attributes or accessible roles.

Example of high-quality selectors:

// Recommended: Test ID attribute
<button data-testid="submit-btn">Submit</button>

// Cypress selection
cy.get('[data-testid="submit-btn"]').click();

// Playwright selection using accessible role
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

Asserts the browser page title in Playwright.

cards.title: Mocking API Requests & Async
cards.content:
E2E tests can run against live APIs (true E2E) or mocked network requests (Stubbed E2E).

  • Live API: High fidelity, but tests can be slow, expensive, or flaky depending on backend availability.
  • Mocked APIs: Extremely fast, reliable, and allows you to test hard-to-reproduce server errors (like 500 Internal Server Error) easily.

Both Cypress and Playwright offer native methods to mock APIs. In Cypress, this is done via cy.intercept(), which allows you to catch fetch requests and return predefined JSON fixtures.

content.instruction: Arrange the steps required to run E2E tests inside a continuous integration (CI) pipeline from first to last:
items: Build the React application production assets.
Spin up a local static server or test environment.
Seed test data or run database migrations if needed.
Execute E2E tests in headless browser mode.
Generate test reports and store video/screenshot artifacts of failures.

content.question: What is a primary cause of 'flaky' (unreliably passing/failing) E2E tests in React, and how should it be resolved?

options.text: Using hardcoded wait timeouts (e.g., cy.wait(5000)); resolve by leveraging automatic retries and waiting for elements to exist in the DOM.
Using CSS modules; resolve by migrating to global Tailwind CSS stylesheets.
Testing in headless mode; resolve by only running tests with visual UI enabled in CI/CD pipelines.
Using React.lazy() for code splitting; resolve by disabling async loading completely in development.

cards.title: E2E Testing Best Practices Summary
cards.content:
To build a resilient E2E testing suite for your React applications, keep these best practices in mind:

  • Decouple from implementation: Don't test React state directly; test what the user sees on the screen.
  • Keep tests independent: Ensure each test runs on its own session. Don't rely on state or database records created by a previous test.
  • Use headless mode in CI: Run tests in the background in your pipelines to save memory and execution time.
  • Fail early: Set up your CI pipeline to run E2E tests on Pull Requests before merging to main branches.
